lesson.lesson_summary: Learners make sure every pronoun points to one clear noun. They spot pronouns with two possible antecedents, vague it, this and they with no antecedent at all, and antecedents that are too far back. They fix each one by repeating the noun or rewriting the sentence. Matching a pronoun to its antecedent was taught in 1-3-13.

learning_objectives.description: Fix a pronoun with two possible antecedents.
success_criteria: Spot the two nouns the pronoun could mean.
Repeat the noun or rewrite the sentence.

learning_objectives.description: Fix vague pronouns with no antecedent.
success_criteria: Replace vague it and they with the real source.

learning_objectives.description: Keep the antecedent close to its pronoun.
success_criteria: Repeat a noun when another noun comes in between.

pages.title: Who Does It Mean?

content.text: A pronoun only helps if the reader can tell which noun it points to. If it could mean two things, or nothing at all, the sentence is unclear.

examples.sentence: Sam told Ali that he had won the quiz.
examples.explanation: He could mean Sam or Ali, so we can't tell who won.

pages.key_takeaway: Every pronoun needs one clear antecedent.

pages.title: Two Nouns, One Pronoun

mistake.incorrect: Mum chatted with Aunt Leela while she was cooking.
mistake.correct: While Mum was cooking, she chatted with Aunt Leela.
mistake.reason: In the first sentence, she could be Mum or Aunt Leela. Naming the cook first makes it clear.

pages.key_takeaway: Two nouns before a pronoun can cause confusion.

pages.title: Repeat the Noun or Rewrite

content.rule_text: If a pronoun could point to two nouns, repeat the noun you mean, or rewrite the sentence so only one noun fits.
content.scope: Pronouns with more than one possible antecedent

examples.sentence: When the dog chased the cat, the cat shot up a tree.
examples.explanation: 'It shot up a tree' could mean the dog. Repeating the cat removes the doubt.

pages.key_takeaway: If in doubt, use the noun again.

pages.title: An It That Points Nowhere

mistake.incorrect: In the newspaper, it says the main road will close.
mistake.correct: The newspaper says the main road will close.
mistake.reason: It doesn't stand for any noun. Make the newspaper the subject instead.

pages.key_takeaway: Name the source instead of a vague it.

pages.title: Who Are They?

content.text: They needs an antecedent too. 'They say' leaves the reader wondering who.

mistake.incorrect: They say it will rain all week.
mistake.correct: The weather forecast says it will rain all week.
mistake.reason: They points to no noun. Name who says it.

pages.key_takeaway: Replace a vague they with the real source.

pages.title: When the Noun Is Too Far Back

content.text: If the antecedent is a long way back, or another noun comes in between, a pronoun may point to the wrong one. Repeat the noun.

examples.sentence: The museum has a dinosaur skeleton and a moon rock. Visitors love the skeleton most.
examples.explanation: 'Visitors love it most' could mean the moon rock, the nearer noun. Repeating the skeleton keeps it clear.

pages.key_takeaway: Keep the pronoun close to its noun.

pages.title: Clear Pronouns: Recap

items: Could it mean two nouns? Repeat the noun or rewrite.
Does it, this or they point to nothing? Name the source.
Is the noun too far back? Use the noun again.
Read the sentence as a stranger would.

pages.key_takeaway: Make sure each pronoun points one way.

question_bank.prompt: Why is 'Priya called Neha after she got home' unclear?

options.text: She could mean Priya or Neha.
She should be her.
Home should come first.

question_bank.explanation: Two girls are named before she, so we can't tell which one got home.

options.text: Rahul was carrying a parcel when he met his grandfather.
Rahul met his grandfather while he was carrying a parcel.
When Rahul met his grandfather, he was carrying a parcel.

question_bank.explanation: In the first sentence, he can only mean Rahul. In the others it could mean the grandfather.

question_bank.prompt: One way to fix an unclear pronoun is to repeat the noun.
question_bank.explanation: Using the noun again shows exactly who or what you mean.

question_bank.prompt: What is wrong with 'They say the new park opens soon'?

options.text: They doesn't point to any noun.
They should be them.
Park should be plural.

question_bank.explanation: Nobody has been named, so the reader can't tell who they are.

question_bank.prompt: Which sentence avoids a vague it?

options.text: The notice on the gate says the pool is closed.
On the notice, it says the pool is closed.
It says on the gate that the pool is closed.

question_bank.explanation: The first sentence names the notice as the subject, so there is no empty it.

question_bank.prompt: If another noun comes between a pronoun and its antecedent, the pronoun may become unclear.
question_bank.explanation: Readers often link a pronoun to the nearest noun, which may be the wrong one.

question_bank.prompt: Read: 'The stall sells kites and lanterns. Grandpa bought one.' Which second sentence is clearer?

options.text: Grandpa bought a lantern.
Grandpa bought it.
He bought one of them.

question_bank.explanation: Naming the lantern shows which of the two things Grandpa bought.

question_bank.prompt: Which word is unclear in 'Leela gave Anu her diary'?

options.text: her
Leela
diary

question_bank.explanation: Her could mean Leela's diary or Anu's diary.

question_bank.prompt: Which rewrite of 'When the glass hit the plate, it broke' is clear?

options.text: When the glass hit the plate, the plate broke.
When it hit the plate, it broke.
It broke when the glass hit it.

question_bank.explanation: Repeating the plate shows which one broke.

question_bank.prompt: A vague this can often be fixed by adding a noun after it, such as 'this delay'.
question_bank.explanation: Adding a noun tells the reader exactly what this means.

question_bank.prompt: Identify the word with no clear antecedent in: 'At the clinic, they told me to rest for a week.'
question_bank.target: The pronoun that points to no noun.
question_bank.explanation: No person has been named, so they is vague. 'The doctor told me' would be clear.

options.text: The baker handed the boy a bun, and the boy grinned.
The baker handed the boy a bun, and he grinned.
He handed him a bun, and he grinned.

question_bank.explanation: In the first sentence, repeating the boy shows exactly who grinned.

cross_references.reason: Introduced in 1-3-1; recalled here in one line.

cross_references.concept: Matching a pronoun to its antecedent

corrections_made: Rewriting questions use multiple choice, because many correct rewrites are possible.
